Amirul Islam with MA Quddus Miah and Most. Shireen Akhter, Advocates ----- For petitioner in Criminal Revision No. 1336 of 1992 and petitioner in Criminal Misc. No. 536 of 1992. 
SS Halder with Probir Halder, Advocates ----- For Opposite party in Criminal Revision No. 1336 of 1992 and petitioner in Criminal Misc. No. 536 of 1992
Syed Matiul Islam, AAG ----- For the State.

full_judgment:
KM Hasan, J.: The Criminal Revision No. 1336 of 1992 and the Criminal Misc. Case No. 536 of 1992 which arise out of the same facts are heard together and disposed of by the judgment. Both the petitions are under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 2. The facts, in short, are that the father of alleged victim girl, Nurunnahar Khanom @ Sima Rani Chakrabarti, as informant lodged the First Information Report on 1.7.92 alleging that on the night following 30th June, 1992 his above named minor daughter aged about 14 years was kidnapped from his bhiti (hut) by the accused Abdul Khaleque and others. Pursuant to that the Kendua PS Case No. 1 (7)92 was intiated under sections 448 and 366A of the Bangladesh Penal Code. 

 5. The father of the alleged victim girl filed an application for the custody of the girl on the ground that she is a minor girl, not yet 14 years old. The application was numbered as Criminal Misc. Case No. 477 of 1992. 

 6. The alleged victim girl also filed a petition on the same date, claiming that she is an adult and 20 years old and understand the realities of life and as such she should not be kept In judicial custody and should be allowed to go anywhere she wants to go. The petition was numbered Criminal Misc. Case No. 501 of 1992. 

 7. The learned Sessions Judge, Netrokona heard the Criminal Misc. Case No. 477 of 1992 and Misc. Case No. 501 of 1992 analogously and by his judgment and order dated 20.9.92 disposed of both the cases with the observation that, "either the victim petitioner or the informant petitioner may prefer an application before the Hon'ble High Court for the release from Judicial Custody, if they so desire." 

 8. The case of the alleged victim girl is that she, being an adult woman and not being an accused or a lunatic, is entitled to live freely. If she is kept in custody under the garb of a Court's order it will be unlawful and illegal. 

 9. Her further case is that her assertions that she has embraced Islam and changed her name and married Abdul Khaleque voluntarily have not been disputed by the opposite party under oath. The Medical Examination report was neither challenged nor denied on the first opportunity. Only thing her father has done is to submit the school certificate to the trial Court to eastablish her age which she claims to be incorrect. The alleged victim girl further claims that her name was published in the final voters list on 15.2.90 in which her age is shown as 18 years and she has cast her vote in the last general election. 

 10. In the meantime the husband of the alleged victim girl Abdul Khaleque filed the case No. 37 of 1992 for the restitution of conjugal rights in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge and the Family Court of Netrokona The girl, through her engaged lawyers, sent a Rafanama dated 19.9.92 with her signature on it, and this was duly attested by the jail authority. In the said Rafanama she has claimed that Abdul Khaleque is her husband and expressed her desire to live with him as his wife. 

 13. The parents also claim that the victim girl had been abducted against her will and she being a minor there cannot be any conversion to Islam or marriage by affidavit as alleged. She cannot also be accused of any complicity because of the same reason. Consequently the position of the victim girl, in the instant case, can only be that of a witness, and as such she cannot be detained in judicial custody and should be released to be returned to her legal guardians i.e. her parents. 

 14. It is admitted on all hands that the girl being a victim and not an accused in the Kendua PS case No. 1(7)92 under sections 448 and 366A cannot be kept under judicial custody. The Court shall either have to return her to the custody of her parents or let her go wherever she wants to go. 

 18. He cites the case of Jahanara Begum alias Jotsna Rani Saba Vs. State and another reported in 15 DLR 148 wherein it has been held, "When a person brought before the court is aged 16 years or over, the will of such person, when the question before the court is whether she (or he) should be detained or allowed to go from Court's custody, must be allowed to prevail. The position of such a person is, at the most, that of a witness and therefore not being an accused she or he cannot be detained against her or his will." 

 19. In the case of Ananda Mohan Banarjee Vs. State, reported in 35 DLR 148, it has been held that the question of custody loses its relevance when the girl concerned is found to be aged over 16 years. She being neither an accused nor a witness in such a case cannot be held in detention under a court's order and is free to go to any place of her liking. 

 20. This view has also the support of the decision held in the case of Manindra Kumar Malakar Vs. Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs reported in 43 DLR 71. 

 22. On the other hand, Mr. SS Haider, the learned Advocate, appearing for the parents, relied on two decisions. They are Sukhendra Chandra Das Vs. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and Krishna Pada Dutta Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, both reported in 42 DLR at 79 and 297 respectively. In these two decisions, Majority Act (IX of 1875) read with Guardians and Wards Act (VIII of 1890) was considered and it was held that in a case of kidnapping under section 366 of the Penal Code, the age would be referable to the age as in the Majority Act and not in the Penal Code. Therefore, the age of 18 years will be the determining factor to decide whether the girl is to be given to the custody of the guardian or not. 

 23. Mr. SS Halder further submits that the leave to appeal (Appeal Nos. 25 & 26 1990) before the Appellate Division against the judgment of the High Court Division in the case of Krishna Pada Dutta Vs. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs has been rejected and the Appellate Division has not disturbed the finding of the High Court Division that the age of sui juris in such a case is 18 years. 

 24. A copy of the judgment rejecting the leave petition by the Appellate Division has been placed before us. It seems that their Lordships in the Appellate Division while rejecting the leave to appeal took the victim girl's age into consideration and found that the girl was below 16 years of age. Their Lordships did not touch upon the question of the age at which a victim girl becomes sui juris with regard to the question of custody in a case of kidnapping. 

 25. Confronted with these conflicting decisions another Division Bench of this court presided over by Mr. ARM Amirul Islam Chowdhury and Mr. Badrul Islam Chowdhury, JJ has considered in detail the question of sui juris in the case of Sumati Begum Vs. Rafiqullah and another, reported in 44 DLR 500. In that case the learned Judges have considered the relevant provisions of the Penal Code along with Children Act 1974 and came to the conclusion that on the basis of section 361 of the Penal Code and section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure a girl reaches the age of sui juris at 16 years of age but at the same time the learned judges opined that where section 55 of the Children Act applies the Court will have the power to keep that child in custody till that child attains the age of 18 years Section 55 of the Children Act deals with a child under 16 years against whom an offence has been committed. 

 26. In another case, Tapash Nandi Vs. The State reported in 45 DLR 26 where an application under section 439 and not under section 491 of the Penal Code is made and where the kidnapped girl is under 16 years and the FIR was lodged under sections 448/366A/109/34 and section 4(a) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Act 1983, a Division Bench or this court has held, "The Penal Code needs to be strictly construed and the offence having attracted the specific provisions of the Penal Code, the age of the victim needs to be determined in accordance with the Penal Code and not with reference to the Majority Act. "It has been further held that where the allegation is that of kidnapping which means taking from the custody of the lawful guardian, namely the parents, sections 361, 366, 366A of the Penal Code will be attracted. The minor to be taken out of custody of the lawful guardian under sections 361 and 366 must be a minor under 16 years of age, and 18 years would be referable only to section 366A when the girl would be taken away for illicit intercourse with another person "and not with the kidnapper. 

 27. It appears that earlier to the above mentioned 42 DLR cases the question, whether the Majority Act will apply in a case of custody of a victim girl in an alleged kidnapping, has also been considered in the case of Fatema Begum @ Urmila Rani Vs. State reported in 9 BLD 469 wherein it has been observed in para 13, "Age limit of 18 years is mentioned for the purpose of marriage only in the Child Marriage Restraint Act. A person cannot be treated as major under the Bangladesh Majority Act unless he or she attains the age of 18 years. This provision has nothing to do with the present case (custody in a kidnapping case) but it has been made for other purpose, namely for the purposes of entering into contracts with others, etc." 

 28. With all these conflicting decisions the question remains at what age does a girl become sui juris. This has not been settled yet. However, it appears from many of these decisions that in case of a dispute as to the age of the girl the court has depended upon its own impression of the girl's age before giving its final verdict. It further appears that in most of these cases, there is no lack of documentary evidence adduced by both sides but the reliability of all the evidence is in question. Decisions have been held by this court according to which Medical and Radiological reports may be off the mark by one or two years. Yet again, there are decisions according to which none of the certificates can be held to be sacrosanct. In the absence of the practice of registration of birth in the official register kept by any public authority, one cannot really be sure of the date of birth of any particular persons. Ultimately, it falls on the court to determine the age of the girl based on the impression received, by her behaviour and appearance when brought before this court. 

 30. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate, has taken us through the victim girl's petition under section 491 of the Penal Code, her statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Annexure B), the report of the radiological expert (Annexure D), the physical examination report of the Medical team dated 12.8.92 (Annexure D), Rafanama" filed in the Case No. 37/92 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and the Family Court, Netrokona (Annexure C) and the voters list (Annexure E). Both in the petition and in her section 164 statement the alleged victim girl has claimed to be 20 years old. The report given by the Radiological expert states that the girl is 16-18 years old. But the Radiological expert has also stated in report, "Before final comment, Physical and Medical Examination should be done" The Medical team in its turn has found the alleged victim girl to be 18 years old. 

 33. Mr. Halder claims that these documents sufficiently and conclusively prove that the girl was minor of 13/14 years at the time of her abduction on 30.6.92 and that at present she has definitely not reached the age of 16 years. He argues that to determine the victim girl's age the school certificate, the mother's affidavit and the horoscope should be relied upon. According to him, the parents are the best persons to know the girl's age and also of their other issues. So the mother's affidavit is the most reliable basis for determining the girl's age. Further, the horoscope is an old one and has been prepared about one and a quarter years after the birth of the alleged victim girl and there is no reason to believe that the date of birth of the victim girl has been misrepresented as early as that for the purpose of this case. Similarly, the school certificate is given by the head master, a disinterested person, and there is no reason why should it not be relied upon for fixing the age of the victim girl. He further argues that the medical report and the opinion of the Radiological expert are not deciding factors as has been decided in various cases (Krishna Pada Datta Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs 42 DLR 297 and Kiran Bala Chowdhury Vs. State 17, DLR 544) and in fact, neither of them give the actual age of the girl. 

 34. In answer to this Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate, submits that there is nothing to show that the horoscope and the school certificate have not been prepared for the sake of the case. In fact the horoscope was not submitted before the learned Sessions Judge. The horoscope and the certificate should not be taken into consideration for fixing the age of the alleged victim girl as it is easy to prepare a horoscope and to procure a school certificate. They are not at all reliable documents for determining the girl's age. 

 35. On this point we have taken into consideration the case of Prafullah Kamal Bhattacharya Vs. Ministry of Home Affairs, reported in 28 DLR 123 wherein it has been held, 

 36. It is always possible to procure a horoscope subsequently for the purpose of using it in a case. It the case of Manindra Kumar Malakar Vs. Secretary of Home Affairs and others reported in 43 DLR 71 it has been observed in para 10, that a horoscope is a private document which may be created at any time for any special purpose. 

 43. It is our opinion that for the purpose of custody in a case of alleged kidnapping the age of the alleged victim girl should not be referred back to the date of occurrence as suggested by Mr. SS Halder. The girl's age at the time of occurrence may be relevant, for the alleged offence committed, but for the purpose of custody the girl's present age is more pertinent. This view of ours is supported by all those decisions where the victim girls have been asked to appear before the court and the question of custody has been decided on the basis of the court's impression of the respective girl's age on the date they appeared before the court. 

 44. In view of the above we make the Rule absolute in Criminal Revision No. 1336 of 1992 and discharge the Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 536 of 1992.
